QF.id: AIFM Fund Monitoring, Reporting, and Exit_11

question.text: At Chenab Ventures' annual LP meeting, an LP asks why the GP received carry even though the fund IRR (pre-fees) is only 11% — below the LP's expected '20% of profit.' Assuming 8% pref, 100% catch-up and 80/20 split were met, the MOST appropriate manager response is:

answer.text: Carry was paid only because catch-up and 20% of distributable profit above pref were achieved; the LP still received its full capital plus 8% hurdle before GP carry began.
Carry is guaranteed to the GP regardless of hurdle; that is standard Indian AIF practice.
SEBI permits carry even where LPs lose money, provided the PPM discloses it.
Catch-up is applied before return of capital, so GP gets carry first and LPs recover later.

explanation.text: The Logic: In a European waterfall, investors first receive return of capital and then the agreed preferred return (here 8%). Only after both are met does the GP receive catch-up distributions until its share of total profit reaches the agreed percentage (20%); residual profit is then split per the agreed sharing ratio (80/20). The Trap: Option B is wrong — Indian PPMs do not guarantee carry irrespective of the hurdle. Option C mis-states SEBI's framework. Option D inverts the waterfall sequence: capital return and preferred return precede catch-up and carry. Note: The fund-level IRR can sit modestly above the hurdle and still generate carry because catch-up and residual sharing apply to the profit above return of capital and preferred return.
